definition: Acting as if you are morally better than other people, in a smug and preachy way.
example: The critic's sanctimonious review scolded readers for enjoying a harmless comedy.
nuance: Unlike sincere moral concern, sanctimonious implies the virtue is put on for show, usually with smugness or a hint of hypocrisy.
prompt: A neighbor comments on how the other people on her street sort their recycling.
options: With a sanctimonious sigh, she announced that she alone bothered to rinse her jars.
Feeling sanctimonious about the weather, she predicted a sunny day for the pickup.
Too sanctimonious to boast, she quietly helped the neighbors on her street sort their bottles.
The sanctimonious bins were scrubbed and disinfected after every single pickup.
reasons: Making a smug show of her own goodness while looking down on others fits the word.
This treats the word like sanguine, which means hopeful; it has nothing to do with optimism.
Quiet, modest helpfulness is the reverse of a showy, preachy display of virtue.
This confuses the word with sanitary; it describes a person's smug attitude, not cleanliness.

practice.prompt: A teenager has just given up sugary snacks for a month.
options: He became so sanctimonious that he lectured his friends about every cookie they ate.
The coach gave a sanctimonious nod, officially approving the new meal plan.
Being sanctimonious, he never mentioned his diet and gladly passed the snacks around.
His aunt praised his sanctimonious honesty when he admitted eating one candy bar.
reasons: Preaching at friends as if his new habit made him better than them is exactly this attitude.
This mixes the word up with sanction, meaning to approve; it does not mean giving permission.
Keeping quiet and not judging anyone is the opposite of smug moral posturing.
The word is an insult, not praise, and humbly owning up to a slip is not smug at all.
